DCRT-Six Cities-3.04
Mr. Mac Mathuna states: “DCRT also has provided no independent data confirming the accuracy
of its assumptions regarding debt cost differentials.” Exh. No. CIT-0018, at p. 12:3-5.

  a. Is Mr. Mac Mathuna aware of FERC approving a “proxy” cost of debt for other
     transmission entities during the construction period prior to raising permanent debt?
  b. If yes, please cite these cases.
  c. Is it Mr. Mac Mathuna’s opinion that FERC has required “independent data confirming the
     accuracy of its assumptions regarding debt cost differentials” in these other cases?
OBJECTIONS:
The Six Cities object to this request to the extent it requests Mr. Mac Mathuna to conduct legal
research for DCRT.
The Six Cities object to this request because it uses an undefined term (“approving”).
Accordingly, the Six Cities object to this request because it is vague, ambiguous, contains words
or phrases that are confusing, or does not identify with specificity the information or material
sought.
The Six Cities also object to this request to the extent that it calls for, or can be interpreted as
calling for, legal conclusions from Mr. Mac Mathuna, a non-lawyer.
Without waiving these objections, the Six Cities will provide a response to this request.
                                                                                         DCT-0345
                                                                                        Page 2 of 2



RESPONSE:
Notwithstanding the foregoing objections, the Six Cities respond as follows:
   a. Mr. Mac Mathuna is not aware of any FERC orders either approving or rejecting the use
      of a “proxy” cost of debt for other transmission entities during the construction period
      prior to raising permanent debt.

   b. N/A

   c. N/A

inquiry.

DCRT-Six Cities-2.11
Mr. Mac Mathuna states: “If the Commission determines that an imputed cost of debt rate is
warranted for use in DCRT’s AFUDC rate notwithstanding Mr. Hoffman’s recommendation, I
would recommend that DCRT use the Moody’s Public Utility Bond Index yield for Baa rated
debt.” (Exh. No. CIT-0018, at p. 17:8-11.)
  a. What is the average maturity of the utility bonds in the Moody’s Public Utility Bond
     Index?
  b. Do the bond yields in the Index include issuance and related costs that a company such as
     DCRT would incur to secure debt?
  c. Is Mr. Mac Mathuna of the opinion that a single-asset transmission company, such as
     DCRT, should be able to raise development period debt capital at the same rate as that for
     diversified mature utilities such as those with long-term debt securities monitored by
     Moody’s in the Baa Utility Bond Yield index?
  d. Can Mr. Mac Mathuna cite any example where a transmission development company, such
     as DCRT, has been able to raise development period debt at a rate comparable to the
     Moody’s Baa Utility bond yield?
  e. If so, please list those examples, including the company, debt raised, and associated interest
     rate in comparison with a concurrent Moody’s Baa Utility bond yield.
OBJECTIONS:
The Six Cities object to this request to the extent that it calls for, or can be interpreted as calling
for, legal conclusions from Mr. Mac Mathuna, a non-lawyer.
                                                                                              DCT-0346
                                                                                            Page 2 of 3




The Six Cities object to this request to the extent it calls for information or documents that are
already in possession of, or equally available to, DCRT.
The Six Cities further object to this request to the extent it requests Mr. Mac Mathuna to conduct
legal research for DCRT.
Without waiving these objections, the Six Cities will provide a response to this request.
RESPONSE:
Notwithstanding the foregoing objections, the Six Cities respond as follows:
   a. Mr. Mac Mathuna understands that the bonds included in the Moody’s Public Utility
      Index have maturities close to 30 years, with an average maturity of 28 years. This
      understanding is informed by the notes section of the attached Mergent Bond Record
      August 2025 report. See the attachment titled PRIV-DCRT-Six Cities-2.011.001.

   b. Mr. Mac Mathuna understands that Moody’s Public Utility Bond Index yields do not
      include debt issuance and other related costs.

   c. This request appears to misinterpret Mr. Mac Mathuna’s recommendation and testimony,
      which reflects a ratemaking construct and not the actual debt instruments that may be
      available to DCRT as a single-asset transmission company. Mr. Mac Mathuna testified
      that DCRT’s cost of debt ratemaking construct is built on numerous unreliable and
      unsuitable assumptions. See Exh. No. CIT-0018 at 9:9 – 11:14. Specifically, DCRT’s
      cost of debt is based on a type of debt that DCRT could not obtain (see id. at 12:2-3), has
      no independent data for support (see id. at 12:3-4), and that DCRT has acknowledged is
      extremely rare (see id. at 12:1-2). Therefore, to the extent “the Commission determines
      that an imputed cost of debt rate is warranted for use in DCRT’s AFUDC rate
      notwithstanding Mr. Hoffman’s recommendation,” Mr. Mac Mathuna recommended
      “that DCRT use the Moody’s Public Utility Bond Index yield for Baa rated debt.” Id. at
      17:8-11.

       Though each public utility, including single-asset transmission companies, will have
       different experiences in securing debt, the selection of the Moody’s Public Utility Bond
       Index Baa yield is reasonable as a transparent and verifiable means of estimating a
       ratemaking cost of debt for DCRT, particularly in light of DCRT witness Mr. Coyne’s
       view of Moody’s Public Utility Bond Index Baa yield as “a conservative estimate of the
       company’s actual credit risk” (Exh. No. DCT-0028 REV at 33:12-13). Further, as Mr.
       Mac Mathuna explained in his testimony, the transmission incentives the Commission
       granted to DCRT, including the hypothetical capital structure, abandoned plant, and
       regulatory asset incentives, serve to reduce DCRT’s risk and help “level the playing
       field” between DCRT and diversified utilities. Exh. No. CIT-0018 at 12:8 – 13:2. In Mr.
       Mac Mathuna’s view, the Moody’s Public Utility Bond Index yield for Baa rated debt is a



                                                  2

       CIT-0018 at 17:13-15.

   d. Mr. Mac Mathuna has not conducted such research.

   e. Not applicable.

                          UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

 DCR Transmission, L.L.C.                                    Docket Nos. ER23-2309-001
                                                                         ER24-1394-001

             RESPONSE OF THE CITIES OF ANAHEIM, AZUSA, BANNING,
                COLTON, PASADENA, AND RIVERSIDE, CALIFORNIA


Requesting Party:             DCR Transmission, L.L.C.
Request Date:                 October 3, 2025
Prepared By:                  Joseph R. Hoffman
Date Sent:                    October 20, 2025


DCRT-Six Cities-2.02
In the approval of DCRT’s declaratory order under section 219 of the FPA, the Commission
approved DCRT’s use of a 50 percent debt and 50 percent equity capital structure.

 a. Is it Mr. Hoffman’s opinion that a hypothetical capital structure, as approved by the
    Commission for DCRT, requires the use of short-term debt for the calculation of AFUDC?
    If so, please explain.
 b. Is Mr. Hoffman aware of cases where the Commission has approved a hypothetical capital
    structure during construction for a new transmission project, and then required a capital
    structure including short-term debt? If so, please cite the specific cases.
OBJECTIONS:
The Six Cities object to this request to the extent that it mischaracterizes Mr. Hoffman’s
testimony.
The Six Cities further object to this request to the extent it requests Mr. Hoffman conduct legal
research for DCRT by seeking citations beyond those already included in Mr. Hoffman’s
testimony.
Without waiving these objection, the Six Cities will provide a response to this request.
                                                                                             DCT-0351
                                                                                           Page 2 of 2




RESPONSE:
Notwithstanding the foregoing objections, the Six Cities respond as follows:
   a. Yes. See, e.g., Exhibit No. CIT-0001 at 9:18-15:3.

       It is Mr. Hoffman’s understanding that all public utilities subject to the Uniform System
       of Accounts (i.e., 18 C.F.R. Part 101) – such as DCRT – are by default required to
       comply with all applicable provisions of the Uniform System of Accounts except to the
       extent that the public utility obtains a waiver of those requirements. The Commission’s
       AFUDC formula expressly contemplates short-term debt balances and rates as inputs to
       the formula. As DCRT acknowledged, DCRT did not seek a waiver of this requirement.
       See Exhibit Nos. CIT-0001 at 12:16-18; CIT-0004 at 62.

   b. This request mischaracterizes Mr. Hoffman’s testimony. Mr. Hoffman testified that
      Commission approval of a hypothetical capital structure for AFUDC purposes does not
      inherently constitute approval of alterations to the AFUDC formula proscribed in the
      Uniform System of Accounts. See Exhibit No. CIT-0001 at 13:1-15:3. As phrased, the
      hypothetical implies that Mr. Hoffman testified that it does necessarily change or waive
      components of the AFUDC formula.
       Nonetheless, Mr. Hoffman is not aware of any cases in which the Commission has
       approved a hypothetical capital structure during construction for a new transmission
       project and then required a capital structure including short-term debt.
Rule 403(c) Certification: Pursuant to Rule 403 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and
Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.403 (2025), I hereby certify that the response to this request is true
and accurate to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief formed after a reasonable
inquiry.
                                                             /s/ JOSEPH R. HOFFMAN
                                                             Joseph R. Hoffman

DCRT-Six Cities-2.06
Mr. Hoffman states: “Given that the purpose of construction financing is construction, it
logically follows that it is proper to treat construction financing debt as short-term debt in the
AFUDC equations, consistent with the Commission’s expectations that such financing would be
the first source of construction financing. Additionally, utilities and the Commission portray
construction financing as a type of financing apart from long-term financing.” (Exh. No. CIT-
0001, at p. 17:5-10.)
 a. What is Mr. Hoffman’s understanding of the mini-perm form of project financing?
 b. Does Mr. Hoffman consider 5-year debt to be long or short-term debt?
 c. Can Mr. Hoffman point to a maturity date in the DCRT Credit Facility that would indicate
    it is short-term debt?
 d. Is Mr. Hoffman aware of other instances where the Commission has treated mini-perm
    financing as short-term debt for purposes of calculating AFUDC? If so, please provide
    relevant citations.
OBJECTIONS:
The Six Cities object to this request because it uses an undefined term (“mini-perm”).
Accordingly, the Six Cities object to this request because it is vague, ambiguous, contains words
or phrases that are confusing, or does not identify with specificity the information or material
sought.
Without waiving this objection, the Six Cities will provide a response to this request.
                                                                                            DCT-0355
                                                                                          Page 2 of 3




RESPONSE:
Notwithstanding the foregoing objection, the Six Cities respond as follows:

   a. In a clarification provided by counsel to DCRT in an e-mail dated October 17, 2025,
      DCRT clarified, “A mini-perm is a specific type of financing commonly used for
      financing energy and infrastructure projects. The question seeks to understand Mr.
      Hoffman’s understanding of the mini-perm model (in part a), and specifically whether it
      is considered short (under 1-year) or long-term debt (in part b).” In response to this
      request as clarified, Mr. Hoffman does not have a specific understanding of the “mini-
      perm” form of financing.

   b. Whether a 5-year debt is considered short-term or long-term depends on a variety of
      factors. As Mr. Hoffman understands it, for example, the criteria for determining
      whether a balance sheet item is short-term or long-term is different depending on whether
      one is referring to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (“GAAP”) or the Uniform
      System of Accounts, which use different criteria for making this determination.

       Furthermore, even if a debt instrument can be properly classified as short-term or long-
       term for accounting purposes, accounting is not controlling of ratemaking. See
       Consolidated Gas Supply Corporation, 14 FERC ¶ 61,029, at 61,053-61,054 (1981). It is
       Mr. Hoffman’s understanding that the Commission applies a degree of judgment in
       assessing how a utility should regard and treat its various debt instruments and prioritizes
       the nature and purpose of the debt incurred, rather than the short- or long-term
       categorization given to the debt for accounting purposes. For example, Southern
       California Edison’s 2024 FERC Form No. 1 identifies a credit facility that it characterizes
       as short-term debt even though the credit facility terminates in May of 2028 (i.e., longer
       than one year). See Southern California Edison’s 2024 FERC Form No. 1, page 122
       (Notes to Financial Statements); page 112-113, line 37.

       Finally, DCRT’s filings with the Commission characterize its construction loan facility as
       debt that will be converted to long-term debt. See Exhibit No. CIT-0001 at 16:17-17:1.
       This indicates that, regardless of whether the construction loan facility is properly
       considered short-term debt, even DCRT does not characterize it as long-term debt.

   c. Mr. Hoffman is unaware of any dates in the DCRT Credit Facility that indicate whether
      the DCRT Credit Facility is the short- or long-term debt. However, as explained in
      response to subpart (b) above, DCRT’s filings with the Commission characterize its
      construction loan facility as debt that will be converted to long-term debt. See Exhibit
      No. CIT-0001 at 16:17 – 17:1. This indicates that, regardless of whether the construction
      loan facility is properly considered short-term debt, even DCRT does not characterize it
      as long-term debt.

   d. Mr. Hoffman is unable to answer this question. See the response to subpart (a) above.
